title: Properties of Power Series
lead: Power series can be added, multiplied by powers of the variable, substituted into, multiplied together and differentiated or integrated term by term, and each operation builds a new power series from known ones. This section works out each operation and what it does to the interval of convergence, and values a lottery prize with a geometric series.
objectives: Combine power series by addition or subtraction.
Create a new power series by multiplication by a power of the variable or a constant, or by substitution.
Differentiate and integrate power series term-by-term.
summary_html:
• Given two power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n}x^{n}$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} d_{n}x^{n}$ that converge to functions f and g on a common interval I, the sum and difference of the two series converge to $f\pm g,$ respectively, on I. In addition, for any real number b and integer $m\ge 0,$ the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} bx^{m}c_{n}x^{n}$ converges to $bx^{m}\kf(x)$ and the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n}{(bx^{m})}^{n}$ converges to $\kf(bx^{m})$ whenever bxm is in the interval I.
  • Given two power series that converge on an interval $(-R,R),$ the Cauchy product of the two power series converges on the interval $(-R,R).$
  • Given a power series that converges to a function f on an interval $(-R,R),$ the series can be differentiated term-by-term and the resulting series converges to $f^{\prime}$ on $(-R,R).$ The series can also be integrated term-by-term and the resulting series converges to $\int \kf(x)\;dx$ on $(-R,R).$

The following exercises explore applications of annuities.

Calculate the annual payouts C to be given for 20 years on annuities having present value ＄100,000 assuming respective interest rates of $r=0.03,r=0.05,$ and $r=0.07.$

answer.solution: In general, $P=\frac{C(1-{(1+r)}^{-N})}{r}$ for N years of payouts, or $C=\frac{Pr}{1-{(1+r)}^{-N}}.$ For $N=20$ and $P=100,000,$ one has $C=6721.57$ when $r=0.03;C=8024.26$ when $r=0.05;$ and $C\approx 9439.29$ when $r=0.07.$

In the following exercises, given that $\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^{n} ,$ use term-by-term differentiation or integration to find power series for each function centered at the given point.

$f(x)=\int_0^{x}\ln tdt$ where $\ln (x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{n-1}\frac{{(x-1)}^{n}}{n}$

answer.solution: Term-by-term integration gives $\int_0^{x}\ln tdt =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{n-1}\frac{{(x-1)}^{n+1}}{n(n+1)} =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{n-1}(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}){(x-1)}^{n+1} =(x-1)\ln x+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{n}\frac{{(x-1)}^{n}}{n} =x\;\ln x-x.$

In the following exercises, using a substitution if indicated, express each series in terms of elementary functions and find the radius of convergence of the sum.

$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{3k}}{6k}$

answer.solution: $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{k}}{k} =-\ln (1-x)$ so $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{3k}}{6k} =-\frac{1}{6}\;\ln (1-x^{3}).$ The radius of convergence is equal to 1 by the ratio test.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, using a substitution if indicated, express each series in terms of elementary functions and find the radius of convergence of the sum.

$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2^{-kx}$ using $y=2^{-x}$

answer.solution: If $y=2^{-x},$ then $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} y^{k} =\frac{y}{1-y}=\frac{2^{-x}}{1-2^{-x}}=\frac{1}{2^{x}-1}.$ If $a_{k}=2^{-kx},$ then $\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_{k}}=2^{-x}\lt 1$ when $x\gt 0.$ So the series converges for all $x\gt 0.$

exercises.prompt: Show that, up to powers x3 and y3, $E(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{n!}$ satisfies $E(x+y)=E(x)E(y).$

answer.solution: Write $E(x)=1+x+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{6}+\cdots$ and multiply $E(x)E(y)$ as two power series, keeping every term of total degree at most 3: $E(x)E(y)=1+(x+y)+(\frac{x^{2}}{2}+xy+\frac{y^{2}}{2})+(\frac{x^{3}}{6}+\frac{x^{2}y}{2}+\frac{xy^{2}}{2}+\frac{y^{3}}{6})+\cdots.$ The terms of each degree are the binomial expansions $\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2!}=\frac{x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}}{2}$ and $\frac{(x+y)^{3}}{3!}=\frac{x^{3}+3x^{2}y+3xy^{2}+y^{3}}{6},$ so up to powers $x^{3}$ and $y^{3}$ the product is $1+(x+y)+\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(x+y)^{3}}{3!},$ which is $E(x+y)$ to that order.

exercises.prompt: Differentiate the series $E(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{n!}$ term-by-term to show that $E(x)$ is equal to its derivative.

answer.solution: Differentiating term by term, $E^{\prime}(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{nx^{n-1}}{n!}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}.$ Putting $m=n-1,$ this is $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{m}}{m!}=E(x).$ The series for $E$ converges for all $x$ (its radius of convergence is $\infty$ by the ratio test), so term-by-term differentiation is valid for every real $x,$ and $E^{\prime}(x)=E(x).$

exercises.prompt: Show that if $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_{n}x^{n}$ is a sum of even powers, that is, $a_{n}=0$ if n is odd, then $F=\int_0^{x}f(t)\;dt$ is a sum of odd powers, while if f is a sum of odd powers, then F is a sum of even powers.

answer.solution: If $f(x)=\sum a_{n}x^{n}$ with $a_{n}=0$ for odd $n,$ then $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k}x^{2k},$ and integrating term by term from 0 to $x$ gives $F(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k}\frac{x^{2k+1}}{2k+1},$ in which every power $2k+1$ is odd. If instead $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k+1}x^{2k+1}$ has only odd powers, then $F(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k+1}\frac{x^{2k+2}}{2k+2},$ in which every power $2k+2$ is even. Integration from 0 adds no constant term, since $F(0)=0,$ and term-by-term integration keeps the radius of convergence, so both statements hold on the interval where the series for $f$ converges.

exercises.prompt: [T] Given the power series expansion $\ln (1+x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n} ,$ determine how many terms N of the sum evaluated at $x=-1/2$ are needed to approximate $\ln (2)$ accurate to within 1/1000. Evaluate the corresponding partial sum $\sum_{n=1}^{N} {(-1)}^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n} .$

answer.solution: When $x=-\frac{1}{2},-\ln (2)=\ln (\frac{1}{2})=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n2^{n}} .$ Since $\sum_{n=11}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n2^{n}}\lt \sum_{n=11}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^{n}} =\frac{1}{2^{10}},$ one has $\sum_{n=1}^{10} \frac{1}{n2^{n}} =0.69306\text{…}$ whereas $\ln (2)=0.69314\text{…};$ therefore, $N=10.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Recall that ${\tan }^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi}{6}.$ Assuming an exact value of $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}),$ estimate $\frac{\pi}{6}$ by evaluating partial sums $S_{N}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ of the power series expansion ${\tan }^{-1}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} {(-1)}^{k}\frac{x^{2k+1}}{2k+1}$ at $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$ What is the smallest number N such that $6S_{N}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ approximates π accurately to within 0.001? How many terms are needed for accuracy to within 0.00001?

answer.solution: $6S_{N}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=2\sqrt{3}\sum_{n=0}^{N} {(-1)}^{n}\frac{1}{3^{n}(2n+1)} .$ One has $\pi -6S_{4}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=0.00101\text{…}$ and $\pi -6S_{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=0.00028\text{…}$ so $N=5$ is the smallest partial sum with accuracy to within 0.001. Also, $\pi -6S_{7}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=0.00002\text{…}$ while $\pi -6S_{8}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=-0.000007\text{…}$ so $N=8$ is the smallest N to give accuracy to within 0.00001.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? In the following exercises, justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If the radius of convergence for a power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_{n}x^{n}$ is $5,$ then the radius of convergence for the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} na_{n}x^{n-1}$ is also $5.$

True or False? In the following exercises, justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

Power series can be used to show that the derivative of $e^{x}\;\text{is}\;e^{x}.$ (Hint: Recall that $e^{x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} x^{n}.)$

answer.solution: True. Differentiate the Maclaurin series of $e^{x}$ term by term: $\frac{d}{dx}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{n!}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{nx^{n-1}}{n!}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{m}}{m!}=e^{x}.$ Since the series converges for all real $x,$ term-by-term differentiation is valid everywhere, and the derivative of $e^{x}$ is $e^{x}.$
